title: AWS Marketplace listing review sync - Redwood Inference (SaaS offer)
customer_attendees: Megan Li (AWS Marketplace Partner Solutions Architect)

summary: AWS Marketplace team walked Redwood through SaaS listing requirements and common rejection reasons. Focus was on security documentation expectations (SOC 2/ISO posture wording, data handling, encryption/KMS, audit logs, retention) and how to present shared responsibility in the listing + attached docs. AWS recommended tightening claims (avoid absolute compliance statements), ensuring support and refund language is explicit, and providing a clean architecture/data flow diagram. Timeline: AWS said first-pass review is typically ~5–10 business days after submission if artifacts are complete; security review can add a few days. Redwood targeted end-of-month submission to support a February launch window, pending final copy, screenshots, and attachment bundle.

transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2026-01-14
Time: 10:03 AM PT
Duration: 43 minutes
Title: AWS Marketplace listing review sync - Redwood Inference (SaaS offer)
Attendees (Redwood): Jordan Blake, Soojin Lee, Chris Osei, Naomi Feldman, Cole Summers, Alex Martinez
Attendees (AWS): Megan Li, Andrew Patel, Sara Kline

Auto Summary (Fireflies)
- Discussed required listing fields and attachments for SaaS offers.
- Reviewed security documentation expectations and compliant wording.
- Covered review timelines, iteration loops, and common delays.


[00:00] Jordan Blake: Cool. Hey everyone, thanks for making the time. Goal today is to make sure we don’t get bounced in the first review cycle. We’re updating our Marketplace listing and we want to confirm requirements, especially security packet expectations and timelines.

[00:17] Andrew Patel: Yep, makes sense. Thanks Jordan. This is Andrew, vendor program side. Megan and Sara are here, Megan on the technical partner SA side, Sara on the security review lane.

[00:27] Megan Li: Hi all.

[00:28] Sara Kline: Hey.

[00:30] Soojin Lee: Hi, Soojin here, product marketing. I’ll probably ask a bunch of “can we say this” questions.

[00:36] Chris Osei: Chris, product ops, tracking submission readiness.

[00:40] Naomi Feldman: Naomi, security and compliance product owner.

[00:43] Cole Summers: Cole from billing/metering.

[00:46] Alex Martinez: Alex, docs/devex.

[00:50] Jordan Blake: Great. Andrew, do you want us to start with the listing itself, or security attachments?

[00:56] Andrew Patel: Usually we start with listing completeness because missing fields can block before it even gets to security. But we can jump around.

[01:04] Jordan Blake: Sure. We’re doing a SaaS offer. Metered for Hosted, and then separate SKUs for Dedicated capacity and Private deployments plus some add-ons.

[01:14] Megan Li: When you say “Private deployments”, are you packaging that as a Marketplace SaaS dimension or is it more like a private offer / contract path?

[01:22] Jordan Blake: Good catch. For AWS Marketplace, we’re thinking public offer for Hosted usage-based, then private offers for Dedicated and Private. The public listing still needs to explain all three, but purchase path differs.

[01:33] Andrew Patel: That is common. Just be careful the public listing doesn’t imply you can click-buy a Private deployment if the actual procurement is private offer and maybe a separate fulfillment.

[01:44] Soojin Lee: Right, we were going to include “Contact us for Dedicated/Private” language. Is there preferred phrasing?

[01:50] Andrew Patel: Something like “Available via private offer” or “Talk to sales to activate” is fine. Avoid “instant provisioning” language if it’s not instant.

[02:02] Chris Osei: On required attachments—what are the hard requirements today for SaaS?

[02:07] Andrew Patel: For SaaS, you’ll need: EULA or terms link, support information (hours, contact methods), refund policy statement, privacy policy, and then any security documentation you want to attach. Also, the “How it works” section has to be clear: subscribe -> get entitlement -> create account or link account -> start using.

[02:27] Megan Li: And architecture diagram is not strictly required, but it’s one of the most common things reviewers ask for when the data handling story is unclear. It’s also helpful for customers.

[02:38] Naomi Feldman: On security docs, are you expecting SOC report attachments? Like the actual SOC 2 Type II pdf?

[02:45] Sara Kline: Not as a public attachment, no. We don’t want vendors uploading full audit reports publicly in the listing attachments. What we typically see is a security overview plus an attestation statement. If you have a SOC 2, you can say “SOC 2 Type II report available under NDA” or “available upon request” and give a process.

[03:05] Naomi Feldman: Ok. We have a security packet that’s “marketplace-ready” with controls summary, data flow, encryption, audit logs, retention, and shared responsibility. Then evidence pointers gated.

[03:17] Sara Kline: That’s the right pattern.

[03:19] Soojin Lee: Can we say “SOC 2 certified”? We currently have that in an older draft.

[03:24] Sara Kline: Please don’t. SOC 2 is an attestation, not a certification. Say “SOC 2 Type II attested” or “SOC 2 Type II report” and keep it factual.

[03:35] Soojin Lee: Got it.

[03:37] Jordan Blake: That’s super helpful, thank you.

[03:40] Megan Li: Also be careful with ISO wording. “ISO 27001 certified” is sometimes ok if you have the certificate and the scope covers the service, but you should specify scope and date. If you don’t want to manage that in the public listing, just say “aligned with ISO 27001 controls” or “ISO 27001 program” but again, be precise.

[04:00] Naomi Feldman: We’ll stick to “aligned” where appropriate and keep hard claims tied to evidence.

[04:06] Chris Osei: Sara, what are the top security reasons a listing gets sent back?

[04:10] Sara Kline: Three buckets. One: ambiguous data handling—where prompts go, whether you store inputs/outputs, and default retention. Two: encryption statements that are too vague, like “we encrypt everything” without in-transit/at-rest detail, or without key management model. Three: claims that imply AWS endorses the service or implies compliance you can’t back up (HIPAA, FedRAMP, PCI, that kind of thing).

[04:35] Jordan Blake: We are getting questions about HIPAA eligibility a lot. We support private/VPC deployments, and we can sign BAAs in certain cases, but it’s not universal.

[04:46] Sara Kline: Then don’t say “HIPAA compliant” on the listing. You can say something like “supports HIPAA-eligible architectures” or “BAA available for eligible customers” if that’s true, but it should be conditional and routed via your sales/legal process.

[05:02] Soojin Lee: That’s consistent with our legal guidance.

[05:06] Megan Li: For the security packet, what we like to see is a simple table: data categories, where they live, retention, and who can access. Also a diagram: customer app -> your API endpoint -> compute plane -> logs/metrics plane. Call out what’s in AWS vs what’s in your own managed service.

[05:29] Alex Martinez: We have a draft data flow diagram. It includes Hosted, Dedicated, and Private variants. Is it ok if the attachment is one diagram with three swimlanes? Or should we keep it one path?

[05:40] Megan Li: Swimlanes are fine, as long as it’s not too busy. The reviewer wants to find “where is customer data” quickly.

[05:49] Sara Kline: And please define your terms: “telemetry”, “application logs”, “prompt logs”. A lot of confusion is whether prompts are in logs by default.

[05:58] Naomi Feldman: Right. Our defaults: we don’t use customer prompts/outputs to train models. We store request metadata for operational purposes; prompt/content logging is configurable, and we have retention controls. We’ll put the defaults and knobs in the packet.

[06:17] Sara Kline: Good. Just be explicit: what is on by default, how long, and how customer changes it.

[06:25] Cole Summers: Quick question on metering dimensions. We’re mapping Hosted usage by tokens, and embeddings by “units”. Dedicated is capacity reservation and may be private offer with committed spend. Does AWS care how we name the dimensions?

[06:38] Andrew Patel: For public offers, yes. The dimension names show up in billing. Keep them customer-friendly and stable. If you change them later, customers notice.

[06:48] Cole Summers: Understood. We found issues before where the internal meter name didn’t match Marketplace, and it caused invoice confusion.

[06:56] Andrew Patel: Exactly. If you can, keep it simple like “Text tokens” and “Embedding units”, and in your documentation specify how it maps to your product metrics.

[07:06] Soojin Lee: Is it acceptable to say “predictable pricing” or “lower cost than alternatives”? We want to highlight cost controls.

[07:13] Andrew Patel: You can say “optimize cost” or “reduce unit cost” but avoid direct competitor callouts like “cheaper than Bedrock” or “half the cost of X”. If you have benchmarks, you can present them, but they must be well sourced and not misleading.

[07:30] Megan Li: And no “AWS approved” type language.

[07:33] Soojin Lee: Yep.

[07:36] Jordan Blake: On screenshots, any specifics? We’re capturing Console views: usage dashboard, token-level latency breakdown, audit log page, and onboarding screen.

[07:46] Andrew Patel: That’s good. Typically 3–6 images. Make sure they’re readable when scaled in the Marketplace UI. Avoid including customer names or sensitive data in screenshots.

[07:58] Alex Martinez: Are there size constraints? We saw 1100 by something in an old doc.

[08:02] Andrew Patel: I’ll send the latest attachment checklist. The portal will also validate dimensions.

[08:08] Chris Osei: Thank you—please do.

[08:11] Jordan Blake: Let’s talk timeline. If we submit end of month, what’s realistic for approval?

[08:17] Andrew Patel: If the submission is complete, first pass is usually 5–10 business days. If security has questions, add a few days. The fastest approvals happen when vendors preemptively attach the security overview, privacy policy, support, refund statement, and a clear “How it works”. The slowest are when things are missing and you go back-and-forth.

[08:41] Sara Kline: And I’ll say: security review itself isn’t always a separate queue, but if we see red flags we’ll ask for clarifications. Each clarification round can take 1–3 days depending on response time.

[08:55] Naomi Feldman: If we give you the security packet as a PDF, is that acceptable?

[09:00] Sara Kline: Yes, PDF is fine. Also links are fine, but if the link is gated behind login, it can slow review. If you need gating, provide a reviewer-access method.

[09:13] Naomi Feldman: We can provide an “AWS-review@” access path or a temporary link.

[09:18] Sara Kline: Perfect.

[09:20] Jordan Blake: We can do that.

[09:22] Soojin Lee: Copy-wise, we’re updating the “How it works” steps. Today it’s too vague. We’ll include: subscribe in AWS -> redirect to Redwood to create or link org -> entitlement check -> API key -> first call.

[09:37] Megan Li: That’s exactly what customers want. Also add troubleshooting: entitlement propagation can take a bit, tell them what error they’ll see and what to do.

[09:49] Alex Martinez: We have a troubleshooting section: “If entitlement not found, wait 10–15 minutes, retry, then contact support with subscription ID.” That ok?

[09:58] Andrew Patel: Yes. Avoid promising exact times but you can say “may take several minutes”.

[10:05] Chris Osei: On refund policy, do we need a specific Marketplace format?

[10:10] Andrew Patel: You need a statement. For usage-based SaaS, many vendors say “No refunds for prior usage” and handle credits case-by-case. Just be clear.

[10:21] Jordan Blake: We’ll align with finance/legal.

[10:24] Sara Kline: Also support. Make sure you list your support hours, response targets if you have them, and escalation path for urgent incidents.

[10:33] Jordan Blake: We have a standard enterprise support SLA with Premium, but hosted self-serve is best effort.

[10:39] Andrew Patel: Then list the standard, and for Premium say “available via private offer” or “contact sales.” Customers hate reading “24/7” and then finding out it’s only for certain tiers.

[10:54] Soojin Lee: Understood.

[10:56] Megan Li: Another common issue: residency. If you mention “EU region” or “data residency”, make sure you specify what it means. Is it request processing region? Log storage? Support access? It’s ok to say “regional processing available” but specify.

[11:14] Naomi Feldman: We have controls for log retention and processing region selection in our Dedicated and Private modes. Hosted is region-limited for now. We’ll make that explicit.

[11:27] Sara Kline: That’s the right approach. Don’t over-claim.

[11:32] Jordan Blake: Quick question about wording: can we say “customer data is not used to train models”?

[11:38] Sara Kline: Yes, if true. That’s common and it helps.

[11:42] Jordan Blake: Great.

[11:44] Cole Summers: In the “How it works” section, can we mention limits/quotas and how they map to SKUs?

[11:49] Andrew Patel: You can. In Marketplace itself, keep it high level. Then link to your docs for exact quota behavior. Customers care because they want procurement to know what they’re buying.

[12:03] Chris Osei: We’re also introducing new SKUs. Any gotchas with changing an existing listing vs creating a new one?

[12:10] Andrew Patel: If you’re replacing a legacy listing, check whether it’s the same product code and whether existing subscribers will be impacted. Often vendors create a new offer and deprecate the old one with a migration plan. But it depends—Megan, do you want to add?

[12:25] Megan Li: Yeah, biggest gotcha is breaking entitlements for existing subscribers. If you change fulfillment URL or product ID, your sync logic must handle both. Work with your Marketplace integration team on that.

[12:37] Jordan Blake: We’re updating our entitlement verification endpoints and sync jobs for that reason. We’ll keep backward compatibility.

[12:46] Sara Kline: From the security side, if the underlying data flow changes materially between old and new offers, update the security attachments accordingly.

[12:55] Naomi Feldman: Yep.

[12:57] Soojin Lee: I’m going to read a sentence from our draft and you tell me if it’s going to get flagged. “Redwood provides enterprise-grade security including encryption everywhere, full audit logs, and compliance for regulated workloads.”

[13:12] Sara Kline: That one would likely get comments. “Encryption everywhere” is vague—say “TLS in transit” and “AES-256 at rest” if that’s accurate, and specify key management (KMS, BYOK). “Full audit logs” is also vague—what events? “Compliance for regulated workloads” is borderline. Say “features to support regulated workloads” and point to your security overview.

[13:34] Soojin Lee: Got it. We’ll rewrite.

[13:36] Megan Li: Plus, “enterprise-grade” is ok as marketing, but reviewers sometimes ask you to back it up. If you keep it, pair it with factual bullets.

[13:46] Alex Martinez: We can change the bullets to: “TLS 1.2+ in transit”, “Encryption at rest with KMS”, “Audit logs exportable”, “Configurable retention.”

[13:56] Sara Kline: That’s better.

[13:59] Jordan Blake: Megan, on shared responsibility, what do you want to see?

[14:03] Megan Li: Simple. A section that says: AWS is responsible for the underlying cloud infrastructure; Redwood is responsible for the service operation and app-layer controls; customer is responsible for what they send, their IAM on their side, and their configuration choices (like enabling content logging). A table is best.

[14:22] Naomi Feldman: We have that in the packet.

[14:25] Sara Kline: Also include sub-processors. If you use any third party for support ticketing, analytics, etc, list categories. Doesn’t need to be exhaustive in the Marketplace attachment, but have a place customers can find it.

[14:40] Jordan Blake: We can point to our subprocessor list page.

[14:43] Andrew Patel: That’s good.

[14:45] Chris Osei: Ok, so to summarize what we’ll send: listing copy, screenshots, “How it works”, support + refund + privacy links, security overview PDF with data flow and shared responsibility, and a reviewer-access approach for any gated docs.

[15:00] Andrew Patel: Yep.

[15:02] Jordan Blake: Anything else we’re missing that commonly trips people up?

[15:06] Andrew Patel: The category selection and keywords. Make sure the headline and first paragraph are clear. Also, don’t bury the procurement path—customers want to know if they can buy self-serve or if it requires private offer.

[15:19] Soojin Lee: We’ll put “Hosted API available as pay-as-you-go; Dedicated/Private via private offer” near the top.

[15:26] Megan Li: Perfect.

[15:28] Sara Kline: And contact emails need to be monitored. If you put “security@” or “support@”, make sure someone answers.

[15:35] Jordan Blake: We’ll use our support alias that’s staffed.

[15:39] Alex Martinez: One more question: Can we attach a link to our docs site for the onboarding steps instead of duplicating everything in the listing?

[15:47] Andrew Patel: You can link, but the listing should still contain the basic steps. Think of it as “minimum viable instructions” in the Marketplace page.

[15:58] Alex Martinez: Ok.

[16:00] Jordan Blake: Great. Andrew, can you send the latest SaaS offer checklist and screenshot guidelines?

[16:05] Andrew Patel: Yep, I’ll send right after.

[16:08] Chris Osei: And if we hit issues during submission, what’s the best escalation path?

[16:13] Andrew Patel: Reply on the case created in the portal and CC me. If it’s blocking, we can pull in the review team.

[16:22] Jordan Blake: Awesome.

[16:24] Naomi Feldman: Sara, if we want you to do a quick pre-check on security packet wording, can we email it?

[16:30] Sara Kline: Send it to Andrew and he can route it, or attach to the case. I can’t promise pre-review outside the workflow, but we can at least tell you if something is a big red flag.

[16:44] Naomi Feldman: That’s helpful.

[16:46] Jordan Blake: Ok, I think we’re in good shape. We’ll target submission by Jan 29.

[16:52] Andrew Patel: Sounds good.

[16:53] Megan Li: Thanks all.

[16:55] Sara Kline: Thank you.

[16:57] Jordan Blake: Thanks everyone.

---
Notes (captured live)
- AWS prefers factual security statements: specify encryption in transit/at rest, KMS model, audit event categories, default retention.
- Avoid “SOC 2 certified” and avoid unconditional “HIPAA compliant” language.
- Provide a clear subscribe -> entitlement -> org link -> API key -> first call flow, plus entitlement delay troubleshooting.
- Expected review lead time: ~5–10 business days for first pass; security questions can add days per iteration.
